title: Silver that owed Lima a passage, and took Buenos Aires instead, 1580 to 1778
register: documentary, and the best evidence is what got confiscated
summary: Silver that the empire's own law sent through Lima and Panama moved south instead, by mule and ox-cart through Jujuy, Salta, and Córdoba to a port with no harbor, where a fabricated shipwreck or a friendly auction turned foreign cloth and captive Africans into legal goods. The corridor ran through governors as often as around them, and in 1776 the Crown stopped trying to suppress it and annexed it instead, folding the old evasion into the new viceroyalty's licensed Atlantic trade.

nodes.name: Potosí
nodes.note: Source of the silver the whole corridor existed to move, and an enormous consumer market in its own right. Four surviving volumes of notarial deeds from 1635–1636 alone record transactions involving 441 enslaved people brought inland through Buenos Aires.

nodes.name: Tupiza
nodes.note: A southern Charcas staging valley providing fodder, rest, and local brokerage between the high plateau and Jujuy.

nodes.name: Humahuaca
nodes.note: Part of the chain of settlements in the Quebrada de Humahuaca carrying goods, animals, mail, and coerced travelers, and the transition zone where cart transport gave way to mules and donkeys.

nodes.name: San Salvador de Jujuy
nodes.note: A chokepoint at the entrance to the Quebrada de Humahuaca, founded in 1593, where carriage shifted from heavy ox-drawn carts to pack animals suited to the climb.

nodes.name: Salta
nodes.note: A major staging, livestock, and mercantile center where mules bred farther south were held and fattened before entering the high-altitude Andean markets.

nodes.name: San Miguel de Tucumán
nodes.note: A market and production node supplying textiles, food, and livestock along the corridor.

nodes.name: Santiago del Estero
nodes.note: A political and ecclesiastical center, and an early node in the Tucumán road system connecting regional production with Córdoba and Charcas.

nodes.name: Córdoba
nodes.note: The principal interior articulation point: a cart-building and livestock market, a credit and redistribution hub, and the site of the dry customs barrier ordered in the early 1620s to tax Buenos Aires merchandise moving north at fifty percent, a barrier goods and silver alike routinely bypassed by known detours.

nodes.name: Santa Fe
nodes.note: Connected the Paraná–Paraguay river system with Córdoba and Buenos Aires, feeding yerba mate, tobacco, and Paraguayan produce into the wider exchange.

nodes.name: Buenos Aires
nodes.note: The Atlantic interface: refounded permanently in 1580, lacking a deep-water harbor so that ships anchored offshore and small craft, carts, and laborers moved cargo under conditions that favored under-declaration. Governors, treasury officers, and cabildo members were as often participants in its commerce as its regulators.

nodes.name: Colonia del Sacramento
nodes.note: Founded by Portuguese forces under Manuel Lobo in January 1680, expelled and restored repeatedly, and finally and permanently taken by Spain in 1777. Confiscation records show at least 877 enslaved Africans seized here between 1740 and 1777, a minimum, not a total.

nodes.name: Montevideo
nodes.note: Founded and settled under Spanish authority in the 1720s, becoming a fortified harbor and customs node that completed, rather than replaced, the multipolar Río de la Plata port complex.

nodes.name: Rio de Janeiro
nodes.note: A principal Brazilian port supplying shipping, credit, enslaved Africans, and re-exported European goods to the Río de la Plata, whose importance varied by period against Bahia and Pernambuco.

nodes.name: Bahia
nodes.note: A Brazilian port supplying credit, sugar, and slave-trade connections; Diego de Vega's early network ran through here as much as through Buenos Aires.

nodes.name: Luanda
nodes.note: An origin point for people forcibly transported into the corridor; the 1594 investigation into unauthorized Buenos Aires commerce specifically accused officials of sending ships here.

nodes.name: Lisbon
nodes.note: A metropolitan endpoint for silver that entered Portuguese Atlantic channels; Fernando Jumar documents 6.4 million pesos of Royal Treasury money reaching Spain via the Colonia–Rio de Janeiro–Lisbon route in the Portuguese fleets of 1747 and 1749 alone.

nodes.name: Lima
nodes.note: The seat of the authorized Pacific route through Callao, Panama, and Portobelo that the southern corridor evaded or circumvented. Lima never held a single statutory monopoly, but its merchants and consulado benefited from rules meant to keep Upper Peruvian bullion from drifting toward the Atlantic.

nodes.name: The Spanish Crown
nodes.note: Prohibited Buenos Aires commerce in 1594, licensed narrow exceptions in 1602 and 1606, prosecuted individual governors for contraband, and in 1776–1778 gave up suppression for legalization, creating the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata and issuing the free-trade regulations. The same authority made the corridor illegal and later made most of it legal.

nodes.name: Diego de Vega
nodes.note: A merchant from Madeira, reconstructed as the central organizer of an intercontinental credit and consignment network connecting Lisbon, Bahia, Buenos Aires, Potosí, and Chile. Calling him 'the first banker of Buenos Aires' is a later interpretive label, useful only functionally.

nodes.name: Juan de Vergara
nodes.note: A Sevillian officeholder, notary associated with the Holy Office, and cabildo figure whose influence exemplifies the overlap of municipal government, ecclesiastical privilege, credit, and contraband. Claims that he 'owned' the cabildo are rhetorical; the documented reality is dominance, not legal title.

nodes.name: The confederados
nodes.note: An early seventeenth-century political-commercial coalition built around Vega and Vergara, opposed by Hernandarias, and allegedly protected by Governor Diego de Góngora.

nodes.name: Hernando Arias de Saavedra, 'Hernandarias'
nodes.note: Repeatedly denounced and prosecuted illicit commerce and became the confederados' political opponent. He was also a colonial governor and a participant in the wider regime of conquest and coerced labor; on the narrower question, records distinguish his enforcement from the commercial participation alleged against several successors.

nodes.name: Diego de Góngora
nodes.note: First governor of the separated Río de la Plata governorship from 1618, accused in his residence proceeding of arriving with illicit cargo and protecting the confederados. Spectacular totals sometimes attached to his case require the original proceeding before being accepted literally.

nodes.name: Jacinto de Láriz
nodes.note: Governor investigated and punished for contraband and other abuses, with property confiscated and penalties reportedly including a fine, banishment, and perpetual deprivation of office.

nodes.name: South Sea Company
nodes.note: Received the 1713 asiento, conventionally summarized as permission to supply 4,800 enslaved Africans annually for thirty years plus an authorized annual merchandise ship. Its Buenos Aires factors were repeatedly accused of contraband; the War of Jenkins' Ear ended effective operation in 1739.

nodes.name: Portuguese Atlantic merchants
nodes.note: Supplied enslaved Africans and European and Brazilian manufactures to a Buenos Aires that could not otherwise pay for them, in exchange for the interior's silver. Their commerce operated through Colonia del Sacramento once it existed and through Brazilian ports before and after.

nodes.name: Acarete du Biscay
nodes.note: Probably a Frenchman of Basque origin who entered Spanish America posing as a Spanish subject and traveled overland from Buenos Aires to Potosí in 1658, conducting trade along the way and reporting the route back for French commercial and strategic interest. His account is the clearest surviving foreign eyewitness case of the corridor operating.

nodes.name: The mita
nodes.note: The compulsory Indigenous labor draft, expanded under the Toledo reforms of the 1570s, that mined and processed the ore feeding the whole corridor. The route cannot be reconstructed honestly as a merchant achievement alone.

nodes.name: Cerro Rico
nodes.note: The silver mountain discovered in 1545 whose output, after mercury amalgamation, was the entire reason a smuggling corridor to the Atlantic was worth building and defending.
